name: Dana Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. Your answers are confidential; what does a normal day on the power lines look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a small repair crew for an electricity company and check every permit before anybody touches a conductor. I have a two-year technical diploma, but the useful knowledge is often which old pole leans after rain.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about leading, and what weighs on you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like getting the crew home with the lights back on. My pay is low for a lead, the mortgage eats most of it, and my partner Sam and I have less than a month of expenses saved for our two schoolchildren.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew we can use a tidier permit, but nobody signs off a line from a screen alone. I have never used an AI tool, and I see no reason to start for a small paperwork saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I would welcome a quiet technology story, but our household is not quiet. One missed pay packet would make the mortgage difficult, and there are few other line crews nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d carry on leading repairs and double-check every printed permit against the switch plan. I’d cut our takeaway meals for the next year and put the difference toward the grocery and mortgage bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about money even if AI hardly changes the work. I know the job well, but skill does not fill an empty savings account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which permit detail would you check first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I check the isolation point and then read it aloud to the second person on the crew. A wrong switch number can leave a line live.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does the takeaway cut free up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam and I spend about sixty a month on it when shifts run late. We would cook ahead on Sundays and use that sixty for the bills.

say: **Line permits** still need a crew check even if routine paperwork becomes quicker.
I would keep leading the **repair crew** rather than adopt an unneeded tool.
think: Our **mortgage** is tight already, and less than a month saved leaves no room for missed pay.
Few **nearby crews** offer a simple escape if hours fall.
do: **Keep** checking isolation points aloud with a second crew member.
**Cut** roughly sixty a month in takeaway meals and use it for household bills.
feel: **Anxious** about existing money pressure, despite the mild AI picture.
S0.quote: I know the job well, but skill does not fill an empty savings account.
fieldNote: Dana’s **thin reserve** drives her mood even when the card brings little change to linework.
Her refusal of **AI tools** is consistent with never using them and seeing no useful task here.

steps.text: Keep checking isolation points aloud before each repair
Cut sixty monthly in takeaway meals for household bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell dispatch that new planning software cannot see a cracked insulator from a desk. If AI starts writing tickets and buying parts, my crew needs the right to send an unsafe ticket back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I fear the office will expect us to clear more jobs without the people to do it. I am the lead and good at fault finding, but lower pay and no cushion mean shorter hours would hurt straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask my manager to put a written stop-work rule on the next crew briefing. I’d keep a paper record of wrong parts on tickets through the first year and ask for corrections before we climb.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious and a little angry at the thought of being rushed. I would rather have an argument over a ticket than a worker hurt on my crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What goes into your paper record?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d write the job number, the part listed, what was actually on the pole, and the time we stopped. That is evidence the next crew can use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the manager says the software is rarely wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the manager to visit a site with us and look at the record. I would not sign off a live-line job just to meet a software target.

say: **AI tickets** may speed dispatch, but crews must be able to reject unsafe plans.
I would take a **wrong part** back to the office before anyone climbs.
think: Higher **work targets** could make our already tight mortgage harder to carry.
My **lead skills** do not protect us if the electricity company cuts paid hours.
do: **Request** a written stop-work rule at the next crew briefing.
**Record** wrong ticket parts and insist on corrections before climbing.
feel: **Anxious** about income and angry at unsafe pressure.
S1.quote: I would not sign off a live-line job just to meet a software target.
fieldNote: She asks for a **written rule**, because an informal promise will not protect a crew under pressure.
The **paper log** fits her cautious habits and offers evidence without requiring AI adoption.

steps.text: Record wrong parts before crews climb

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my crew full thinking AI by 2028 may run the office, but people will still repair lines until capable robots arrive around 2031. I would demand a live demonstration before the electricity company lets a robot near our crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect a smaller crew after those robots arrive and I do not have three years of savings to wait. There are few lineworker jobs nearby, so I cannot say I would simply walk into another company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask my manager this month for a written staffing plan through the robot trials. I’d cut our summer trip now and ask the mortgage lender what reduced payments would require if my hours actually fell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am alarmed, because I can picture losing a large part of my pay. I can keep the crew safe today, but I cannot promise another lineworker job in this town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about the trip?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell our two children the summer trip has to become days out near home. I would not blame them or promise a replacement date I cannot pay for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What exactly would you ask the lender?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask what documents they need if my paid hours drop and whether any temporary arrangement is possible. I would not assume they will approve one.

say: **2028 thinking AI** changes office work before capable line robots around 2031.
I would require a **live demonstration** before robots work near my crew.
think: I expect a **smaller crew** after robots, with less than a month of expenses saved.
Few local **lineworker jobs** make a quick replacement wage unlikely.
do: **Ask** the manager for a written crew staffing plan this month.
**Cancel** the summer trip and choose local days out instead.
**Ask** the mortgage lender about requirements if paid hours actually fall.
feel: **Alarmed** about a likely large pay loss and very little financial room.
S2.quote: I can keep the crew safe today, but I cannot promise another lineworker job in this town.
fieldNote: Her **lead status** does not erase the immediate risk of thin savings and a limited local job market.
The lender enquiry is **conditional**; she does not claim a payment reduction has been granted.

steps.text: Cancel the summer trip for local days out
Ask the lender about options if paid hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say thinking AI in 2031 and capable robots around 2034 give us a little more time to prove what is safe. I would still want a person leading each repair until a proper field test shows otherwise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years gives Sam and me time to lower the mortgage, if our pay holds. I would consider training to inspect robot work only if the company pays for it and keeps my wage during the course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d pay an extra forty toward the mortgage in months with paid storm shifts. I’d also ask the training lead this year whether a paid inspection course and a real post are planned, then wait for an answer before enrolling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, though less trapped than in the fast picture. A longer calendar helps only if the wages to use it keep coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why forty rather than more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Forty is about what remains after a storm shift once the bills are covered. I will not promise it every month when the shifts are uncertain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there is no paid inspection post?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading repairs and keep asking for the company’s staffing plan. I would not spend our last savings on a course with no job attached.

say: **2031 thinking AI** precedes capable repair robots around 2034.
I would keep a **human lead** on each repair until field tests prove a safe method.
think: Five years might let us **reduce debt** if storm pay continues.
A robot inspection course needs **company pay** and a real post before I enroll.
do: **Pay** forty extra on the mortgage in months with paid storm shifts.
**Ask** the training lead about a paid inspection course and post this year.
feel: **Anxious**, but a little less trapped if paid work continues.
S3.quote: A longer calendar helps only if the wages to use it keep coming.
fieldNote: Her **extra payment** depends on newly earned storm pay, not on shifting the existing reserve.
Training remains an **enquiry**, contingent on funding, wage protection and a genuine post.

steps.text: Pay forty extra on the mortgage in paid storm months
Ask about a paid inspection course and real post

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew thinking AI in 2036 and capable robots around 2039 leave time for proper safety rules. A decade is enough to test machines on dead lines before asking families to trust them on live repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be in my fifties by then, but I cannot talk about retiring early with our mortgage and tiny reserve. If my company keeps a human crew lead, I would rather stay at the job I know than gamble on a new trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep leading the repair crew and write down the faults that only a site visit reveals. This year I’d ask my manager to review our lower lead pay against the responsibilities, and use any actual raise first to build an emergency fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the distant change but anxious about today’s bills. Ten years of warning does not pay next month’s mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which fault would you put in the notebook?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would note a loose connector hidden behind a cover that looked sound from the ground. The notebook would show why a crew still has to inspect the metal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your manager denies the raise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the job and look for permitted overtime before promising new savings. There are too few nearby line teams for me to resign over one pay conversation.

say: **2036 thinking AI** and robots around 2039 allow a long safety test period.
I would document **hidden faults** that only a site visit catches.
think: Our **mortgage** and tiny reserve rule out an early retirement plan.
I prefer a **human lead** role to an unfunded leap into another trade.
do: **Keep** leading repairs and document faults seen on site.
**Request** a review of lead pay against responsibilities this year.
**Build** the emergency fund only if a real raise arrives.
feel: **Anxious** about current bills despite a long technology timetable.
S4.quote: Ten years of warning does not pay next month’s mortgage.
fieldNote: Her **present money pressure** remains even when the scenario delays robots by a decade.
The **emergency fund** is conditional on an actual raise, and she does not assume management will grant one.

steps.text: Keep leading repairs and document hidden faults
Build emergency savings if a raise arrives

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because our reserve is too small to survive a sharp cut in crew pay before we can find other work. A written staffing plan, paid training tied to an actual post, and clear stop-work authority would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the people writing the robot plan what a lower-paid crew lead is meant to live on while the trials run. A technical diploma does not cover a mortgage payment by itself.

headlineQuote: A technical diploma does not cover a mortgage payment by itself.
portrait: Dana is a forty-three-year-old **crew lead** with a technical diploma, two children, a mortgage and less than a month saved.
Her **lower pay** and few nearby lineworker jobs make even mild scenarios anxious for the household.
She has never used **AI tools** and relies on permits, spoken checks and a paper fault log.
Fast robots leave her **alarmed**; more time helps only if paid work and any funded inspection role are real.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut crew pay before her household has enough savings or another local job.
whatWouldHelp: A written **staffing plan**, paid training tied to a post and clear stop-work authority would help.
